title: When the Kitchen Breaks
premise: Quentin Reyes has built a career on other people's voices, ghostwriting a celebrity chef's memoirs while hiding the truth that she once wrote a decade of anonymous letters to the man who now lives next door: August Hale, a former restaurateur whose kitchen—and life—collapsed years ago. As the memoir deadline looms, Quentin discovers the memoir's subject is entangled in the same scandal that destroyed August, forcing her to choose between the loyalty she owes her employer and the truth she owes the man she loves. When August learns she was his letter-writer and that her book may bury him, their fragile second chance shatters; Quentin must burn her professional reputation by telling the truth, and in the final chapter, a reopened neighborhood kitchen—hers and his—becomes the place where they finally stop hiding.
about_author: Theo Villalobos spent seven years as a line cook in Portland before trading service windows for writing desks, a history that seasons every page with the smell of scorched butter and second chances. He writes love stories about people who are better with their hands than with their words.

chapters.title: Mise en Place
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She ghostwrites a triumphant chapter for celebrity chef Marisol Vance, then comes home to find a moving truck next door and a man carrying a crate of dented copper pans. Recognition hits like heat. The beat: quiet dread beneath ordinary routine.

chapters.title: The Letters I Never Signed
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, flashback-woven. Ten years ago she wrote anonymous letters to August Hale, a rising chef, signing them only 'Q.' Now he lives twenty feet away and doesn't know her face. The beat: longing tangled with cowardice.

chapters.title: Borrowed Sugar
chapters.summary: August's POV. He knocks on Quentin's door to borrow a whisk, and something about her voice snags a memory he can't place. They talk about kitchens, not names. The beat: tentative warmth, an almost-recognition.

chapters.title: Deadline Season
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Marisol's memoir hits its crunch; the manuscript must expose the 2015 kitchen scandal that ended August's career—Marisol's version of it. Quentin realizes she'll be the pen that buries him. The beat: the first real crack between loyalty and truth.

chapters.title: Sunday, Simmering
chapters.summary: August's POV. He cooks a slow ragù and Quentin ends up at his table, the first meal they've shared in a decade. He tells her the scandal ruined him unfairly; she says nothing about her manuscript. The beat: intimacy built on an omission.

chapters.title: What Marisol Wants
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Marisol pressures her to make August the villain of chapter twelve, dangling the byline Quentin has secretly craved her whole career. Quentin stalls. The beat: temptation with teeth.

chapters.title: Handwriting
chapters.summary: August's POV. Sorting old boxes, he rereads the 'Q' letters and notices the loops in the handwriting on a casserole dish Quentin returned look familiar. He starts testing her, gently, with questions about words she uses. The beat: hope sharpening into suspicion.

chapters.title: Two Kitchens, One Fire
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A shared-block cookout; August and Quentin cook together for the first time, wordless and easy, and neighbors tease them like an old married couple. That night she almost confesses everything—letters, book, name. The beat: the almost.

chapters.title: The Villain Chapter
chapters.summary: August's POV. Marisol, doing press, publicly revisits the scandal and names August as the saboteur. He spirals; Quentin comforts him, hating herself. The beat: guilt wearing the mask of tenderness.

chapters.title: Ghostwriter's Confession (Unsent)
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She drafts a letter to August confessing everything—the letters, the memoir, her name—and can't send it. Marisol calls: finish the chapter or lose the credit. The beat: the noose tightening.

chapters.title: The Recipe Card
chapters.summary: August's POV. He finds an old recipe card in Quentin's kitchen written in the 'Q' hand. He doesn't confront her; instead he cooks her mother's dish from memory, watching her face. She knows he knows. Neither speaks. The beat: suspended heartbreak.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Counter
chapters.summary: August's POV. He asks her directly: were you Q? She admits the letters but hides the memoir. He's radiant with a decade of answered longing—and she's drowning. The beat: joy and deceit sharing one small kitchen.

chapters.title: Chapter Twelve, Drafted
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Under contract threat, she writes August's ruin in Marisol's voice, then reads it aloud to an empty room and hears only lies. The beat: self-betrayal made concrete on the page.

chapters.title: Marisol's Version
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV (single departure). We learn her side: her fear, her ambition, and a detail suggesting the scandal's true saboteur was someone else entirely. The beat: the enemy rendered human, the mystery deepened.

chapters.title: The Leak
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. An advance excerpt of the memoir leaks; August reads himself named as the villain—and learns Quentin ghostwrote the book. He connects the letters, the lies, the byline. The beat: everything Quentin feared, arriving at once.

chapters.title: What You Signed Your Name To
chapters.summary: August's POV. The confrontation: he forgives the letters, cannot forgive the book. 'You gave me a decade and sold me in a chapter.' He returns her casserole dish, empty. The beat: the breaking.

chapters.title: Burning the Draft
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She refuses Marisol's final edits, pulls the villain chapter, and offers to testify about what she found in the archives—Marisol's business partner falsified the health records that destroyed August. Marisol threatens to ruin her. The beat: the whole heart, finally risked.

chapters.title: The Archives
chapters.summary: August's POV. Quentin shows him the evidence she uncovered: the real saboteur's paper trail. He learns she chose truth over the byline she'd wanted her whole life. The beat: anger softening into awe.

chapters.title: Public Record
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. The truth goes public; Marisol's publisher delays the memoir, Quentin's agency drops her, and her name appears—for the first time—on a correction that vindicates August. The beat: costly, necessary ruin.

chapters.title: Service Window
chapters.summary: August's POV. He asks Quentin to help him reopen a tiny neighborhood kitchen, not as Q the letter-writer or the ghostwriter, but as Quentin. She says yes before he finishes the sentence. The beat: forgiveness as a door left open.

chapters.title: First Night Open
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The kitchen's opening night: chaotic, joyful, August cooking, Quentin running the pass, neighbors filling every seat. Between courses, he hands her a letter—his first to her, signed with his full name. The beat: visibility as love.

chapters.title: Signed, Quentin
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, epilogue. She begins writing her own book under her own name, first line about a man and a whisk. August reads over her shoulder; she lets him. The beat: a life no longer borrowed, a voice finally her own.
